# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Critical reading of the 24-month follow-up of Varden and Halden

This is a strong follow-up, and it settles several questions the earlier documents left open:

- **Durability:** the per-hour gain persisted to 24 months, under randomisation with record-based output.
- **Unrecorded work:** the authors added an hours measure from system log data that doesn't depend on staff claiming time.
- **Meetings:** they tested the meetings mechanism under a registered plan.
- **Waiting times:** these are now compared against control offices, which fixes a gap in the nine-month report.
- **The meta-analysis's decay claim:** they show that the long-follow-up studies behind it were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, as I suspected when reviewing it.

There are still problems. The summary misstates the size of the decline, control offices partly took up the intervention, the hours measured from logs don't reconcile with the meeting figures, and the Halden section has some issues of its own.

## What holds up

### The arithmetic is correct

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Output per hour, timesheets, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8% |
| Output per hour, system logs, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5% |
| Halden subset, 11 continuing organisations | 96.8 / (34.9 / 40.3) = 96.8 / 0.866 = +11.8% |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 = 100% |

### The response to the "entirely an artifact" claim holds

Varga and Holm called for record-based output, actual hours, a control group and long follow-up. This trial meets all four standards and still finds +8.5% (CI +3.4 to +13.8). The authors also credit the re-analysis fairly where it was right.

### The novelty prediction was tested and failed

Fatigue is still 0.34 SD better at 24 months, and the per-hour gain is still clearly above zero. Varga and Holm's prediction that energy would return to baseline around month ten is not borne out.

### The wellbeing results are durable

Sick days are −27% at 24 months against −29% at nine. Resignations show the same gap as before. Sickness absence is now the most robust finding in this literature: randomised, two years long, and replicated.

### The counter arm's end is informative

The county ended reduced hours in counter offices for a stated, quantified reason: waits of 7.3 against 4.0 minutes, and 12% more staff needed to restore service. The coverage-bound conclusion is now supported by the employer's own decision as well as the data.

## Problems

### 1. The summary compares figures from two different measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data." But the 12.5% was measured on timesheets. Logs were not collected at nine months.

The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% to **9.8%**, both on timesheets. Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" has the same problem:

- **Like-for-like (timesheets):** 12.5% to 9.8% is a decline of about **a fifth** (22%).
- **Across measures:** 12.5% to 8.5% is a decline of about a third (32%).

"About a quarter" matches neither.

### 2. The decline isn't statistically established

The confidence intervals overlap heavily: +6.9 to +18.4 at nine months, and +4.6 to +15.2 at 24 months. No test of the difference is reported. "Consistent with some fading" is a fair description. Treating the decline as established is not.

### 3. Control offices partly adopted the intervention

The authors mention the month-15 "meeting audit" in two control offices only as a hint that reorganisation alone might help. It also contaminates the comparison:

- Two of the seven control offices improved output per hour by about 4.1%. Averaged over seven offices, that raises the control mean by roughly **1.2 percentage points** for months 15 to 24.
- The difference-in-differences shrinks accordingly. That could account for **up to about half** of the 2.7-point like-for-like decline.
- The audit plausibly happened because the nine-month report publicised the meetings finding. That is spillover through knowledge of the trial, which office-level randomisation was meant to prevent.

So part of the apparent "fading" may be the control offices improving, not the treated offices falling back. The authors should report the 24-month estimate both with and without those two offices, and say whether the audit was prompted by the trial.

The control meeting figures also need checking. If two of the seven offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, the reported control average of 7.2 to 7.0 implies the other five *rose* by roughly half an hour on average. That is possible, but the paper should state it.

### 4. The hours from system logs don't reconcile with the meeting cuts

The log measure is described as time "working on cases". Meetings presumably don't count as log time. Now look at the hours:

- Timesheet hours fell by about 12%, roughly **4.5 hours** a week from a baseline of about 37.9.
- Meeting time fell by about **3.3 hours** relative to control (−3.5 in treated, −0.2 in control).
- That leaves only about 1.2 hours of the reduction for everything else, case work included.
- Yet case-work time, from the logs, is reported to have fallen by **11%**. On any plausible base of case-work hours, that is about 3 hours.

Meetings plus case work then account for well over the total hours cut. Something doesn't fit. Either log-in time includes time spent in meetings, or log time and timesheets cover different scopes, or other work rose.

This matters for two reasons:

- **The headline figure.** Calling the logs the "stricter" measure assumes they measure the same thing as timesheets, only better.
- **The mediation result.** If meetings are outside the log denominator, cutting them doesn't mechanically raise output per log hour. A 47% meetings share would then imply an indirect effect, such as fewer interruptions to case work. That is a stronger and more interesting claim than "time was removed," and the paper should say which it means.

### 5. The mediation result is weaker than "confirms"

Registering the test before seeing 24-month outcomes is a real improvement. Still:

- **Only the treatment was randomised, not the mediators.** Offices whose managers cut meetings may also have changed other things, such as management quality or prioritisation. The limitations section acknowledges the assumption of no unmeasured confounding. But the summary's "confirms" is stronger than the method allows.
- **Effective sample size.** "A larger sample of office-months" still means 14 clusters. If office-months were treated as independent, the CI of 28–66% is too narrow. The paper should say how clustering was handled.
- **The test was not fully blind.** It was registered at month 11, after the authors had seen the month-six meetings correlation. That is legitimate, since registration came before the outcome data, but the hypothesis came from this same trial.

"Survives a registered test" is fair. "Confirms" is too strong.

### 6. The Halden section has selection and baseline issues

- **Further selection.** Fourteen of the 23 organisations agreed to take part, on top of the selection already described. The authors honestly call the result an upper bound, which is appropriate.
- **The baseline may be borrowed.** The 40.3-hour baseline is exactly the 27-organisation figure from Varga and Holm. The 11 continuing organisations should have their own baseline. If 40.3 was used for them, the +11.8% is computed against the wrong denominator. It's also unclear whether all 11 have time-tracking data, since only 17 of the 23 did.
- **The reversion is stretched to fit.** The summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations." One was a marketing agency citing client deadlines, which is discretionary work under the meta-analysis's coding. Calling it coverage-bound makes the story tidier than the data. One discretionary organisation reverting is a useful finding and should be reported as such.
- **The attrition charge goes unanswered.** Okafor, a Halden author, co-signs this report. Varga and Holm alleged that Halden misdescribed its nine withdrawals: seven left after the schedule began, mostly citing problems keeping up output. This was the most serious charge in the re-analysis, and the report doesn't address it.

### 7. Smaller points

- **Hours are creeping back up.** Timesheet hours fell 13% at nine months but only 12% at 24 months. That is a small upward drift worth tracking.
- **Output per employee.** At −3.4% (CI −8.0 to +1.2), output per FTE has moved slightly further below control. It isn't statistically significant, but on full pay it is a cost trend the county will notice.
- **Who evaluates the hypothesis.** The authors are testing a mechanism they proposed themselves. Registration mitigates this, but independent replication would carry more weight.
- **Source of baseline meeting data.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only at month six. The baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2 hours) were presumably retrieved later from calendar histories. The paper should confirm this.

## Where the five documents leave things

| Question | Best current evidence | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Halden's +23.4% | Inflated by design and measurement | High |
| Gain per actual hour in discretionary work | About +8–10% at 24 months in the randomised trial; up to about +12% in self-selected survivors | Moderate, up from before |
| Durability | Persists to 24 months, perhaps with some decline. The decline isn't significant and may partly reflect control contamination | Moderate, up from low |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Not supported | High |
| "No decay" (meta-analysis) | Not supported by its own evidence, though the Varden data don't establish decay either | Moderate |
| Output per worker in discretionary work | About −2% to −4%, not significant | Moderate |
| Coverage-bound work | Output falls, service worsens, staffing cost up about 9–12%; the employer ended it | High |
| Mechanism | Meetings plausibly the largest single pathway, with fatigue secondary and about a third unexplained. Rests on one trial with 14 clusters and non-randomised mediators | Low to moderate |
| Gain without cutting hours | Two contaminated control offices hint at it; untested | Low |
| Sickness absence | About −27–31%, durable to 24 months, randomised | High |
| Halden's attrition reporting | Still unanswered | n/a |

The next design to run is the one the authors themselves identify: a three-arm trial with reduced hours, meeting reorganisation at full hours, and a control group. It would answer the question that now matters most for employers: how much of the gain comes from cutting hours, and how much from the reorganisation the hours cut prompts.
